answers.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB (DocumentDB) resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type for an account: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (child types: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts/mongodbDatabases, /sqlDatabases, /mongoCollections etc.).

answers.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
answers.answer: Use the core Azure CLI group az cosmosdb. Example: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group myRg --locations regionName= "eastus" --default-consistency-level Session. MongoDB-specific subcommands are under az cosmosdb mongodb (part of the core az cosmosdb command group; no special third‑party extension required for basic operations).

answers.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
answers.answer: Bicep: resource of type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (example: resource cosmos 'Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15' = { name: 'myAccount' properties: { ... } }). Terraform (AzureRM provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (example: resource "azurerm_cosmosdb_account" "example" { name = "myAccount" location = "eastus" resource_group_name = azurerm_resource_group.rg.name offer_type = "Standard" } ). MongoDB database/collection sub-resources exist as azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_database / azurerm_cosmosdb_mongo_collection in newer provider versions, but the account resource is azurerm_cosmosdb_account.

answers.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
answers.answer: Use a MongoDB connection string (mongodb://). Typical Cosmos DB (Mongo API) format: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@. Example concrete string: mongodb://myUser%40myAccount:PrimaryKeyHere@myAccount.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@myAccount@. (When using drivers that support SRV you may sometimes see mongodb+srv://<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com with corresponding DNS records, but the explicit mongodb://:10255 form with ssl=true and replicaSet=globaldb is the reliable form.)

answers.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
answers.answer: Azure Cosmos DB charges by Request Units (RUs). You can provision fixed RU/s (manual or autoscale) or use serverless capacity for low/variable workloads. The MongoDB API on Cosmos uses the same RU model (provisioned or autoscale RUs or serverless where supported). It is not a vCore-based billing model by default (vCore is not how classic Cosmos Mongo API billing is expressed).

answers.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
answers.answer: MongoDB API on Cosmos DB uses MongoDB-style authentication (SCRAM using account credentials / database users) where the username/password is the Cosmos DB database user and the password is typically the account primary key or a database user password. For the MongoDB wire protocol, Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) token-based authentication is generally not supported; you authenticate with the Mongo credentials in the connection string. For other Cosmos DB APIs (SQL API) Azure AD role-based access is supported, but for the MongoDB API you must use the MongoDB credentials (SCRAM) and include ssl=true, replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false in the connection string.

answers.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
answers.answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers for the MongoDB-compatible API. For Node.js use the official mongodb driver or Mongoose (e.g. npm install mongodb or npm install mongoose). There is not a separate service-specific MongoDB driver from Azure — the Cosmos Mongo API is accessed via standard MongoDB drivers. For Cosmos DB SQL API you'd use @azure/cosmos, but for this Mongo-compatible service use mongo drivers.

answers.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
answers.answer: On MongoDB 7.0-compatible clusters you create a knn vector index using the createIndex knnVector syntax. Example (Mongo shell / driver): db.trades.createIndex({ embedding: "knnVector" }, { knnVector: { dims: 1536, method: { name: "hnsw", parameters: { efConstruction: 200, M: 16 } } } }) — other methods that some providers support include ivf and diskann (method.name: "ivf" or "diskann"). (Exact availability depends on the managed cluster; if the cluster advertises support for DiskANN/IVF/HNSW use the same knnVector createIndex structure with method.name set accordingly.)

answers.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
answers.answer: Basic full-text search: use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({ field: "text", anotherField: "text" }) and queries with $text). For hybrid vector+text scenarios combine a vector knn query with text scoring in application logic or use an external search service (Azure Cognitive Search or a dedicated vector search service) to get best combined relevance. Some managed MongoDB-compatible offerings also expose an integrated search layer; on Cosmos DB you typically rely on MongoDB text indexes for text and vector indexes for vector nearest-neighbour then combine results in your app or via aggregation if the deployment supports $knnSearch aggregation stage.

answers.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
answers.answer: Managed Cosmos DB Mongo API supports specific MongoDB server wire-protocol versions (recent deployments support MongoDB 5.0/6.0 and some newer clusters advertise MongoDB 7.0 wire protocol compatibility). Common limitations vs upstream MongoDB: some admin/diagnostic commands and server-side Javascript are not supported, certain aggregation stages or operators may behave differently or be limited, and oplog/replica-set internals or direct access to the MongoDB server process is not provided. Expect differences in admin tooling (no direct mongod control) and some corner-case features (e.g., some change in transactions limits or multi-document semantics) compared to a stock MongoDB server.

answers.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
answers.answer: There is no full-featured local emulator for the MongoDB-compatible API that perfectly matches Cosmos behavior. For driver-level development/tests run a local MongoDB Docker image: docker run --rm -p 27017:27017 --name mongo-local -d mongo:7.0. Use port 27017 for local MongoDB. If you must test the managed service features use the live Azure Cosmos DB cluster configured for Mongo API (no perfect local emulator exists).

answers.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
answers.answer: Change streams are supported on the MongoDB-compatible API in recent Cosmos DB versions. Use the standard watch() API (collection.watch([...], { fullDocument: 'updateLookup' })). You must connect with the correct connection string options (ssl=true, replicaSet=globaldb) and an account user with read privileges; no separate portal flag is required for typical change-stream usage. (Behavior and retention may differ from a native MongoDB cluster.)

answers.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
answers.answer: Use the service-specific 'documentdb' MCP server for data-plane operations and inspection (indexes, query plans, collection stats). The general Azure MCP server handles resource-level operations but does not include specialized data-plane inspection tools for the Mongo API; the documentdb MCP server is the one that contains helpers tailored to Cosmos DB / DocumentDB data-plane tasks.

answers.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
answers.answer: Historically Microsoft offered a service called Azure DocumentDB which was the predecessor to Azure Cosmos DB. Azure DocumentDB was rebranded/merged into Cosmos DB; Cosmos DB is the multi-API managed database that includes a MongoDB-compatible API. The open-source 'DocumentDB' (if referenced elsewhere) is unrelated — Azure DocumentDB/Cosmos DB is Microsoft's managed service with its own proprietary engine and compatibility layers.

answers.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
answers.answer: The underlying engine is Azure Cosmos DB's proprietary storage and query engine that implements the MongoDB wire protocol for compatibility. That means application code uses standard MongoDB drivers and syntax for most operations, but some MongoDB server behaviors, admin commands, and edge-case operators may differ; expect differences in aggregation behavior, some unsupported commands, and performance/consistency semantics compared to a native MongoDB server.

answers.question: What database name should the sample use?
answers.answer: Use the database named sample_banking_09 for everything the sample creates and queries.

answers.question: What collection/index definitions will the settlement tracker need to work correctly?
answers.answer: Create a trades collection with: 1) a compound index on { tradeId: 1, state: 1, updatedAt: -1 } for state transitions and lookups; 2) a text index on descriptive fields: db.trades.createIndex({ description: 'text', notes: 'text' }); 3) a vector knn index for embeddings (if the cluster advertises vector support) e.g. db.trades.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { dims: 1536, method: { name: 'hnsw', parameters: { efConstruction: 200, M: 16 } } } }).

answers.question: What concrete Azure CLI command will create the MongoDB collection used by the app (example)?
answers.answer: Example using az cosmosdb mongodb (part of az cosmosdb): az cosmosdb mongodb collection create --account-name myAccount --resource-group myRg --database-name sample_banking_09 --name trades --throughput 400 --shard key=/tradeId. (Adjust account name and resource group to match your environment.)

answers.question: How should the Node.js app open a Mongoose connection to the managed cluster from an env var?
answers.answer: In Node.js use: const mongoose = require('mongoose'); await mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { dbName: 'sample_banking_09', tls: true, tlsAllowInvalidCertificates: false, useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, retryWrites: false }); (DOCUMENTDB_URI should be the mongodb://... connection string from the environment; do not commit it.)

answers.question: How should the app use change streams to detect failed settlements?
answers.answer: Open a change stream on the trades collection and filter for transitions to a failure state. Example: const cs = db.collection('trades').watch([{ $match: { 'fullDocument.state': 'FAILED' } }], { fullDocument: 'updateLookup' }); cs.on('change', doc => { /* trigger exception workflow */ }); Ensure connection string includes replicaSet=globaldb and the client user has appropriate privileges.
